elements.char: The main contributions of this work to the existing nicotine PBPK model are three-fold. First, nicotine dosimetry
elements.label: text

elements.char: distribution (BC, GI, or other RT compartments) resulting from using different nicotine-containing products that
elements.label: text

elements.char: result in different systemic routes of exposure is more realistically captured. Second, usage conditions (frequency
elements.label: text

elements.char: and duration of use, intensity of use such as puff volume for aerosol inhalation or squeezing of oral products,
elements.label: text

elements.char: swallowing and spitting frequency) are more accurately estimated. Third, the anatomical and physiological dif-
elements.label: text

elements.char: ferences between the URT and LRT and their effects on the rate of nicotine permeation to the bloodstream are
elements.label: text

elements.char: accounted for. The entire nicotine release and transfer rates consisting of several phenomena that are partially

elements.char: To incorporate these processes in the PK profile predictions, three types of models are needed: (1) Dosimetry
elements.label: text

elements.char: models predict the uptake distribution of the available nicotine in the BC, GI, URT, and LRT. In PK studies, the
elements.label: text

elements.char: dosimetry information is key to correlate observed clinical results with the delivered dose. The dosimetry models
elements.label: text

elements.char: are primarily driven by the route of exposure, making them more dependent on product specific parameters,
elements.label: text

elements.char: thereby requiring specific dosimetry models for different types of nicotine containing products. (2) Permeation
elements.label: text

elements.char: model, allows for calculating the rate of nicotine transfer to the circulation system in each of the three regions,
elements.label: text

elements.char: depending on the type of the product. The same permeation model is applied to all products, with differences
